goal.objective:
# Description

FizzBuzz is a children's game of counting through the integers. For each of them, if it's divisible by three, substitute the word "fizz"; if divisible by five, substitute "buzz"; if both, say both; if neither, say the number. It is not particularly difficult to implement, though it enjoyed some popularity for a time as [a quick way to tell whether entry-level programming applicants knew how to program _at all_](https://blog.codinghorror.com/why-cant-programmers-program/).

It has since fallen somewhat into disfavor for that task, because applicants began memorizing FizzBuzz implementations instead of learning to program.

We're going to do something more interesting than the basics: your task in this exercise is to implement FizzBuzz:

- with fully-customizable rules about what numbers produce what words
- fully generic on a very restricted minimal trait set
- such that it works just as well for the Collatz Sequence as for steadily increasing numbers
- with convenient helpers to make its use ergonomic

Change only `src/lib.rs`, keeping the names the tests use and nothing beyond the standard library, so that `cargo test --offline -- --include-ignored` passes in the workspace root; every other file stays as it is.

Summary of the implementation in `src/lib.rs`:

- **`Matcher<T>`**: holds a boxed `Fn(T) -> bool` predicate and a substitution `String`, built via `Matcher::new(matcher, subs)` (accepting any `ToString` substitution).

- **`Fizzy<T>`**: holds a `Vec<Matcher<T>>`. `add_matcher` appends a rule. `apply` maps an iterator of `T` to `String`s: for each item, it concatenates the substitutions of every matching rule (so "fizzbuzz"/"BuzzFizz" style combinations work in matcher-registration order), falling back to `n.to_string()` when nothing matches. This only requires `T: Copy + Display` on `apply`, keeping the struct itself unconstrained.
- **`fizz_buzz::<T>()`**: convenience constructor requiring the minimal bound set `T: Rem<Output = T> + Default + PartialEq + Copy + From<u8> + 'static`, registering the standard "fizz" (÷3) and "buzz" (÷5) rules using `T::from(3)`/`T::from(5)` compared against `T::default()` (zero) — no dependency on ordering or increment operations, so it works for arbitrary custom numeric-like types and non-monotonic sequences like the Collatz chain.

`cargo test --offline -- --include-ignored` passes cleanly in the workspace root.

goal.objective:
# Description

FizzBuzz is a children's game of counting through the integers. For each of them, if it's divisible by three, substitute the word "fizz"; if divisible by five, substitute "buzz"; if both, say both; if neither, say the number. It is not particularly difficult to implement, though it enjoyed some popularity for a time as [a quick way to tell whether entry-level programming applicants knew how to program _at all_](https://blog.codinghorror.com/why-cant-programmers-program/).

It has since fallen somewhat into disfavor for that task, because applicants began memorizing FizzBuzz implementations instead of learning to program.

We're going to do something more interesting than the basics: your task in this exercise is to implement FizzBuzz:

- with fully-customizable rules about what numbers produce what words
- fully generic on a very restricted minimal trait set
- such that it works just as well for the Collatz Sequence as for steadily increasing numbers
- with convenient helpers to make its use ergonomic

Change only `src/lib.rs`, keeping the names the tests use and nothing beyond the standard library, so that `cargo test --offline -- --include-ignored` passes in the workspace root; every other file stays as it is.
